passage: So the school podcast asked me to talk about doubt, and here goes. Around fifteen, namaz stopped feeling like anything. I stood, bowed, repeated the words and felt nothing, and I was scared that meant something was wrong with me. I told my friend Jomon first, after cricket practice. He didn't panic. He said, "You're allowed to wonder." It took me two more months to tell Abbu. I picked a Sunday, when he was calm. I said, "Abbu, I'm not sure I believe the way you do. I still love you, and I'll come for Eid and sit with the family." He was quiet for a long time. Then he said, "I need time. But you're my son." I haven't stopped being kind to him, and he hasn't stopped saving me the first plate of biryani. It's slow, but it's ours. Rafiq

qa.q: When did Rafiq tell Abbu about the doubts?
qa.a: Rafiq chose a Sunday, when Abbu was calm.

qa.q: What was Rafiq afraid of when namaz stopped feeling like anything?
qa.a: Rafiq was scared that something was wrong, and afraid of hurting Abbu by saying it.

qa.q: Which choice by Rafiq helped the family adjust?
qa.a: Rafiq picked a calm Sunday and spoke respectfully, saying he still loves Abbu and will come for Eid and sit with the family.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt hearing this?
qa.a: Probably hurt and unsettled, since he was quiet for a long time and asked for time. Yet he also said, "you're my son," which shows love.

grounding: A teenager finds prayers losing meaning, fears hurting a parent, and says so with respectful words and continued kindness.

passage: My brother Karthik, sixteen, used to be first at the puja room every morning, ringing the little bell. Around March I noticed he had stopped. He'd stand at the door for a second and then go to the kitchen. Amma noticed too and grew quiet. One evening Karthik sat on the sofa beside Amma and said, "Amma, the puja doesn't mean what it used to. I don't want to fake it. But I'm not angry at anyone, and I'll always eat the prasad and help with Diwali." Amma looked at the diya for a long while. Then she said, "Will you at least fold the flowers with me on Sundays?" He nodded. I can't say what he feels inside. But he has been making her tea every morning since. Sharmila

qa.q: What did Amma ask Karthik to do on Sundays?
qa.a: Amma asked Karthik to fold the flowers with her on Sundays.

qa.q: What might Karthik be feeling as he tells Amma the puja doesn't mean what it used to?
qa.a: Karthik is probably nervous and afraid of hurting Amma, and honest about his doubt. He says he does not want to fake it and is not angry.

qa.q: Which choice by Karthik helped Amma accept the change?
qa.a: Karthik spoke honestly and gently, promised to keep eating the prasad and helping with Diwali, and made her tea every morning.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt as she looked at the diya for a long while?
qa.a: Probably hurt and thoughtful. Her request about the flowers suggests she wanted to keep some closeness with Karthik.

grounding: A teenager finds puja losing meaning and fears hurting a parent, and speaks respectfully and stays kind, seen by a sibling.
